newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: FOCUS-EU rejects farm price compromise, seeks new one.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU rejects farm price compromise, seeks new one.

text.p: European Union farm ministers on Tuesday rejected a compromise EU farm price package because of plans to slash aid to wealthy wheat farmers, and asked Dutch Farm Minister Jozias Van Aartsen to prepare a new one.

The compromise was also unacceptable to EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler because he said he could not be bound by a demand for cereals set-aside to be fixed at an unchanged five percent in 1998/99.
A Dutch EU Presidency spokesman said that further bilateral talks will be held after which Dutch Farm Minister Jozias Van Aartses will present a new compromise text early on Wednesday.
"In past years the first compromise has never been the final one and at least two have been needed," the spokesman said. "We shall try to get an agreement during civilised working hours."
The annual EU farm price package has traditionally been agreed only after at least one all-night negotiating session.

Only Britain, Sweden and Denmark backed the Dutch plan and an agreement still looked remote after a European Commission spokesman said that Fischler was sticking to his guns and insisting that cereals aid should be reduced.

On Monday, an overwhelming majority of ministers attacked a proposal to cut payments to cereals farmers by 1.4 billion ecus ($1.6 billion) to help fund aid for beef producers hit by the mad cow crisis.
They disputed Fischler's claim that cereals farmers were over-compensated for cuts in support prices and said there was enough spare cash in the 1997 farm budget to help beef farmers.

Fischler insisted the aid could be adjusted to match price changes and added that there was no room in the 1998 budget to compensate farmers after a fall in beef prices due to the health scare over bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).
"Fischler is sticking to the arable aid cut," his spokesman Gerard Kiely said. "Every attempt has been made to take on board member states wishes but they only come back asking for more."
Fischler said he was disappointed with ministers' expensive "wish lists" which complicated what was an otherwise straightforward package of mainly unchanged prices.
Most of the concessions that don't cost money have been made, Kiely said, adding, "The shop is nearly closed."

The Commission argued it was too early to fix the rate for set-aside -- a scheme intended to remove costly grain mountains, under which farmers must take a certain percentage of their land out of production to obtain EU subsidies.
"We need all the (crop) data before we can fix the set-aside rate," Kiely told reporters.
Earlier, French Farm Minister Louis Le Pensec told journalists: "Seeking a solution will not be easy. We are still a long way from agreement."
